title: 5 Myths About Day Trips From Stari Grad, Croatia
metaDescription: Day trips from Stari Grad, Hvar: Hvar Town by bus, Pakleni Islands, Vis and the Blue Cave, Split, Jelsa. Real prices, times and what to skip.
content:
## Myth 1: Hvar Town is too far away to be a day trip

**The myth:** Hvar Town sits across the island, so it needs a rental car or an expensive taxi.

**The reality:** The two towns are about 17 km apart by road. The island bus between them takes roughly 20-30 minutes and costs about €2-4 one way. It usually meets ferry arrivals, but frequency drops sharply in autumn and winter, and service is not guaranteed in shoulder season. A taxi from the ferry pier to Hvar Town costs about €30-45, which is poor value for a trip a bus handles.

**Better alternative:** Take the morning bus, spend the day in Hvar Town, and return by the last bus. Check the posted timetable at the Stari Grad bus stop the day before. In Hvar Town, the Fortress (Španjola) above the harbour is the one paid sight worth the climb. The main square (Pjaca) and the Arsenal are free to walk through.

This is usually not worth the extra cost: a private transfer between the two towns. Save the money for the boat day.

## Myth 2: The Blue Cave is the day trip you cannot skip

**The myth:** A trip to Hvar is incomplete without the Blue Cave on Biševo.

**The reality:** The Blue Cave day from Hvar costs €100-120 per person for 8-10 hours on the water. The cave ticket is separate and paid on the spot: €24 per adult from 20 June to 10 September, €18 outside that window. The boat ride inside the cave lasts about 5-10 minutes. The light effect works best roughly 11:00-13:00, and trips run only when the sea is calm. Bad weather often cancels or reroutes the day, and many boats arrive in the same two-hour window, so there can be a queue at the cave.

The full tour also includes stops that can be worth the time: the Green Cave on Ravnik (about €6-12 depending on season), Stiniva Cove, and swimming stops near Vis. Together they fill a full day, which is why many operators bundle them.

**Better alternative:** If the cave itself is the draw, book it for a calm-weather day and keep the weather window flexible. If you want a boat day without a long sail, the Pakleni Islands (see Myth 3) deliver swimming for a fraction of the cost. The Blue Cave is worth it only if you value that single 10-minute experience more than a relaxed day. Many visitors rate the beaches and swim stops higher than the cave.

## Myth 3: Boat tours only work if you stay in Hvar Town

**The myth:** Because the Vis and Biševo tours leave from Hvar Town, staying in Stari Grad rules them out.

**The reality:** Group tours typically depart Hvar Town around 10:30. Some operators advise leaving earlier, around 9:00 or 9:30, to get ahead of the group boats. From Stari Grad this means catching the first bus, arriving with a buffer, and checking the return bus time before you board. A tour that returns after the last bus leaves you with a taxi bill of €30-45.

**Better alternative:** For a shorter boat day, use the Pakleni Islands, a chain of wooded islets just off Hvar Town. Taxi boats run from the Hvar Town harbour to Palmižana on Sveti Klement, the largest island, and to nearby bays. This is a half-day trip, needs no all-day commitment, and avoids the weather risk of open-water crossings to Vis.

**Insider perspective:** Stari Grad residents and boat operators treat the first bus as the key constraint, not the boat. Confirm the return bus when you book, not when you land.

## Myth 4: Split is a pointless trip from Stari Grad

**The myth:** Split is the departure city, so going back for a day is a waste of a Hvar stay.

**The reality:** Stari Grad is the only Hvar port with the Jadrolinija car ferry (line 635) to Split. The crossing takes about 1 hour 50 minutes. In 2026 high season (29 May to 27 September), a foot passenger pays €8.40. Off-season the fare is €5.90. A car costs €47.60 in high season and €35.60 off-season. There is also a catamaran, around 1 hour, at about €9.70. This makes it the cheapest day trip on the island. The ferry docks about 2 km outside the old town, so allow time to walk or take a taxi to the pier.

The constraint is the return. Sailings run roughly every few hours in summer and drop to three or four per day in October. A day in Split requires confirming the last sailing back to Stari Grad before you leave. Missing it means paying for a Split hotel.

**Better alternative:** Spend the day on Diocletian's Palace, the Riva waterfront and Marjan hill, then head back with a buffer of at least an hour. Skip the Split markets and shops if the schedule is tight. Do not try to combine Split with Trogir in the same day on a ferry timetable.

Save your money here and spend it on something better: do not book a Split-based guided tour that starts from a Hvar hotel. The ferry already does the job.

## Myth 5: Everything worth seeing is in Hvar Town

**The myth:** Hvar Town is the only place on the island worth a day trip.

**The reality:** The island has two other small towns on the same northern coast that people overlook. Vrboska, a few kilometres east of Stari Grad, is a small harbour village known as the 'little Venice' of the island, with a canal and a fortified church. Jelsa, further east, is a larger resort with a long waterfront promenade and pebble beaches, and it sits on the same bus line. The south coast and the far east of the island have quieter coves, but most are only reachable by car or boat.

**Better alternative:** Combine Vrboska and Jelsa in one half-day by bus or bike. A bike is practical on the road to Vrboska, which is short and mostly flat. The road to Jelsa has more climbs. Both towns have restaurants with grilled fish and local wines at lower prices than Hvar Town.

**Insider perspective:** Hvar Town's prices peak July to August. Day-trippers who want a similar harbour atmosphere at lower cost usually find it in Jelsa.

## What to Book First When Staying in Stari Grad

Lock in the transfers before the tours. The Hvar Town bus and the Split ferry both have limited departures, and either can end a plan by missing a return. Decide the main trip first: Blue Cave and Vis if the weather is calm and the budget allows €125-145 per person with the cave ticket and lunch extras; Pakleni Islands if a half-day swim is enough; Split if cost matters most. Check the timetable for the specific travel date, because summer and autumn schedules differ sharply. Book the cave tour with free cancellation, since sea conditions can change the plan overnight.

faq.question: But isn't Hvar Town only reachable by taxi from Stari Grad?
faq.answer: No. The island bus runs between the towns, about 17 km, taking roughly 20-30 minutes for about €2-4. A taxi is the expensive option at about €30-45.

faq.question: Isn't the Blue Cave included in the tour price?
faq.answer: Generally no. Boat tours cost about €100-120 per person, and the cave ticket is paid separately on the spot: €24 per adult from 20 June to 10 September, €18 outside that window. The Green Cave is another separate fee.

faq.question: Can I do a Split day trip without a car?
faq.answer: Yes. The Jadrolinija car ferry takes foot passengers for €8.40 in high season and €5.90 off-season. The crossing is about 1 hour 50 minutes. Check the return sailing before you go, especially in autumn.

faq.question: Is the Blue Cave tour worth the money?
faq.answer: For many visitors it is a long day for about 10 minutes in the cave. It suits people who want a full boat day with swim stops at Vis, Stiniva and the Green Cave. If you only want swimming, the Pakleni Islands cost much less.

faq.question: Do I need to leave from Hvar Town for the Vis and Blue Cave tour?
faq.answer: Yes, for most group tours, which depart Hvar Town around 10:30. From Stari Grad, take an early bus and confirm the return time before booking.

faq.question: Are there good day trips that do not need a boat?
faq.answer: Yes. Vrboska and Jelsa are on the island's northern coast and are reachable by bus. Hvar Town and its fortress are a bus ride away as well.

faq.question: Does weather affect these day trips?
faq.answer: Yes, mainly the boat trips. Blue Cave tours run only on a calm sea and can be changed or cancelled in bad weather. Ferry and bus schedules are less affected, but check sailings in rough conditions.

quickAnswer: Many visitors assume Stari Grad is a poor base for day trips because the big boat tours leave from Hvar Town. In fact, the Hvar Town bus costs a few euros, the Split ferry is the cheapest crossing on the island, and the Blue Cave day works from here with one early transfer.
